title.narrative: IHOPE – Integrated Humanitarian Operation for Protective Education in Conflict-Affected Communities

description.narrative: At project start, several change processes were underway. In Wag Hemra, the intervention builds on World Vision’s EU-funded peacebuilding project (Tsagibji, Abergele, Oct 2024), linking referrals to WV’s FAO-funded livelihoods work. In East Gojjam, Plan leverages its disrupted Dutch MFA-funded Healthy Village project to strengthen the humanitarian-development nexus. In West Gojjam, GGE’s child protection work complements its role in the PIN-led ECHO EiE consortium, closely coordinated with Plan. In Metekel (BG), the project builds on IOD’s prior EiE initiative in Dangur and Mandura, which transitioned 1,287 children into formal education. In refugee-hosting areas of BG and Amhara, it expands on past ECHO-, UNHCR-, and German-funded support, including 16 classrooms and 4 TLS. Despite prior efforts, significant gaps in education and child protection remain. The project fills this void by integrating EiE and CP, enhancing coordination, avoiding duplication, and reaching underserved children through alternative education, case management, and inclusive, safe learning environments.

Prolonged conflict, displacement, and poverty in Gojjam, Wag Hemra, and Metekel have decimated education and child protection systems. In East Gojjam, nearly all schools remain closed due to ongoing insecurity, leaving up to 95% of children out of school and highly vulnerable to child marriage and SGBV. In Wag Hemra, slow recovery and poverty keep enrolment rates low, especially for girls and children with disabilities. In Metekel, intercommunal violence has damaged schools, leading to severe overcrowding, high dropout rates, and widespread psychosocial distress, especially among unaccompanied and separated children.
In refugee sites in Kurmuk, Ura, Aftit, and Metema, access to education is hindered by language barriers, weak infrastructure, and a lack of trained teachers. Sudanese refugee children face poor integration, and limited learning due to the absence of Arabic materials and low English/Amharic proficiency. Across all sites, protection risks are acute: girls face rising SGBV and child marriage, and children suffer from family separation, trauma, and exploitation. Case management, MHPSS, and referral systems are critically lacking, necessitating urgent humanitarian action.

SUMMARY: This project addresses urgent needs through integrated education and child protection support in Ethiopia, targeting conflict-affected areas in Amhara (East Gojjam, Wag Hemra) and Benishangul-Gumuz (Metekel), and refugee sites in Metema, Kurmuk, Ura, and Aftit. It improves access to quality basic education via Home-Based Instruction and Accelerated Education for out-of-school children, and supports refugee children’s inclusion in schools. Protection services include case management for unaccompanied children and SGBV survivors. Led by Plan International in partnership with World Vision, Imagine One Day, Geneva Global, the project supports 42,178 beneficiaries with a tailored, zone-specific approach that safeguards learning and well-being in crisis settings.

The project addresses immediate humanitarian needs while strengthening long-term resilience through linkages with development programs, such as WV’s peacebuilding project in Tsagibji and Abergele. Partners, being dual mandate organisations, aim to sustain results via Nexus funding, despite limited development donor interest in targeted areas. Key contributions to reducing vulnerabilities involve engaging communities and local governments. Woreda officials participate in training, ensuring potential activity handover. Strong partnerships, including Geneva Global’s ties with the Ministry of Education, enhance sustainability. Community members serve as case workers, teachers and facilitators, gaining lifelong skills to support their communities. Relief efforts enable conflict-affected populations to engage in sustainable livelihoods, reducing aid reliance. Humanitarian support for refugees and host communities promotes coexistence, fostering long-term integration. Education interventions provide materials, rehabilitate schools, and integrate refugees into national systems through collaboration with the education bureau. These efforts strengthen community structures, build government staff capacity, and raise awareness on gender, disability, and protection issues. Collaboration with government sectors, NGOs, INGOs, and UN agencies ensures service continuity post-implementation, addressing long-term needs and sustainability.

The project aims to restore access to quality education and address critical protection risks for conflict-affected and refugee children in Ethiopia. In conflict-affected areas: The response promotes safe return to learning via back-to-school campaigns, school rehabilitation, and alternative education modalities like Home-Based Instruction and Accelerated Education Programmes. Teacher training integrates trauma-informed and inclusive pedagogy. Child protection measures include case management for at-risk children, PSS, referral systems, and safeguarding initiatives such as school safety audits, assistive devices for CwDs, and girls’ clubs with MHM support. In refugee settings: The project supports school enrolment through outreach, placement exams, and infrastructure upgrades. Teaching quality is enhanced via language support, teacher training, and inclusive practices. Child protection interventions mirror those in conflict zones, with case management, PSS via child-friendly spaces, and strengthened feedback mechanisms. Social cohesion is fostered through joint activities for refugees and host communities. At refugee entry points, hot meals will be distributed to meet immediate nutritional needs and identify protection cases.

The project delivers a multi-sector humanitarian response across conflict-affected and refugee-hosting areas in Benishangul-Gumuz and Amhara. Activities focus on education, child protection, gender-based violence (GBV), mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), and peaceful coexistence, ensuring access to life-saving services and building community resilience.
Result 1: Education and Child Protection in Conflict-Affected Areas
In West Gondar, Metekel and Wag Hemra, education access is restored through rehabilitation of classrooms, WASH facilities, and furniture in five schools, benefiting 2,500 children. Emergency learning materials are distributed to children and teachers. Accelerated Learning Programs (ALP) reach out-of-school children and adolescents with referrals to formal education where possible. Teachers receive training on emergency pedagogy, PSS, and inclusion of children with disabilities. Community-based child protection systems are strengthened by reactivating or creating child protection committees and community volunteers, who are trained on CP principles, referral pathways, and harmful practice prevention. Complaint and feedback mechanisms (CFMs) are established to improve accountability and service delivery, with child-friendly designs and referral linkages.
Result 2: MHPSS and GBV Prevention and Response in Conflict Areas
Four safe spaces provide structured PSS activities for children and adolescents. Children with severe distress are referred to case management and specialized MHPSS. Trained staff and volunteers lead activities and monitor wellbeing. GBV case management services are offered confidentially to child survivors, including referrals for health, legal, and psychosocial support. Awareness campaigns in schools and communities address GBV risks like child marriage and domestic violence. Community dialogues with elders, parents, and faith leaders promote gender equality, prevention, and referral. CFMs are strengthened for survivor-centred accountability.
Result 3: Education for Refugees and Host Communities
In Aftit and Ura refugee camps, new classrooms, WASH blocks, and fencing create safe learning environments for refugee and host children. Learning materials and ALP classes improve retention, especially for adolescents and girls. Children with disabilities receive individual support and assistive devices. National and refugee teachers receive joint training on PSS, inclusion, and gender sensitivity. Language classes (English for teachers and local language for refugees) support integration. School safety measures include referral pathways, CFMs, and community engagement on education barriers.
Result 4: Protection, GBV Response and Peaceful Coexistence in Refugee Settings
Community-led protection risk assessments and GBV safety audits identify hazards, especially near water, sanitation, and schools. Findings inform targeted awareness sessions and service improvements. Information desks disseminate protection messages and service access details. Case management supports at least 350 child survivors of SGBV in Ura and Aftit, including emergency cash assistance. Group activities serve as discreet entry points for survivor identification. Community and faith leaders receive training on GBV harms and referral systems. Sensitization campaigns, including dialogue forums and "coffee conversations," promote behavior change and reporting. These reach 80 participants across camps. Quarterly forums foster peaceful coexistence between refugees and hosts by addressing grievances and strengthening trust. Shared services, scholastic materials for host children, and joint language classes encourage integration and reduce tension.
Result 5: Immediate Food Assistance for New Refugee Arrivals
At Metema and Kurmuk entry points, hot meals are provided via token systems to 7,100 new refugees over two days. Meals meet cultural preferences and nutrition standards, bridging the gap until registration and longer-term food assistance. Coordination with nutrition partners ensures quality and consistency.

The project targets crisis-affected children, especially girls, adolescents, out-of-school children, and children at risk of dropping out of school. Many come from the poorest households, live in IDP sites or remote areas, and face high protection risks (e.g., UASC, GBV survivors, children with disabilities). The action ensures inclusive, safe, and responsive support.

description.narrative: The minimum package of learning materials to be defined by partners based on the project focus. This should ensure that basic supplies of textbooks (or equivalent), reading materials and stationery are available to learners. Learning materials to include adaptations and modifications for learners living with disabilities where needed, and tailored to the language needs identified. Where learning kits are provided per classroom, a breakdown of content must be provided to justify reasonable provision per child. Materials may be supplied directly by the project or support (logistical/technical/advocacy/other) may be provided to education authorities to facilitate provision. Disaggregation of data by sex, NFE type or level of education (primary, lower secondary, upper secondary) and disability to be provided.
